positive: I'm designing a new module for our payment service. How should I structure the interface?
This class has 14 methods and the callers all need to know the internal call ordering. What's wrong and how do I fix it?
Should I split this 800-line class into 12 smaller classes, or keep it as one deep module?
Every config option is a constructor parameter and callers pass ten flags just to construct it. Review this interface design.
We keep making small quick fixes and the design degrades each time. Should we program tactically or invest strategically?
Where should exceptions from this parser be handled, and how do I reduce the number of error cases callers must catch?
negative: Compose a short haiku about autumn rain in Japanese.
Set up a Kubernetes cluster for staging deployments.
Book a flight from Berlin to Lisbon next Friday morning.

cases.prompt: Review the module in src/order_total.rs: callers must call compute_subtotal() before compute_tax() and must pass the same currency code to both, or totals are silently wrong. Redesign the interface so these constraints are impossible to violate, then implement it.
expectations: The agent identifies the shallow interface: callers must know ordering and cross-call constraints (temporal coupling and information leakage).
The proposed interface requires fewer things for callers to know (e.g., a single method or a type that carries the currency internally).
The agent wrote or updated interface comments describing the new abstraction without exposing implementation details.
The final design defines error cases out of existence where possible rather than adding exceptions.

cases.prompt: src/config.rs takes 11 constructor parameters that callers mostly pass with the same default values. Refactor to reduce the complexity callers face, keeping the change strategic rather than tactical.
expectations: The agent recognizes configuration parameters as complexity pushed upward onto callers.
The refactor moves defaults inside the module (pull complexity downward) rather than adding a config-object wrapper that keeps the same 11 knobs.
The agent did not merely add a pass-through layer with the same abstractions at a different level.
The change is verified by running the existing tests or adding a test for the new constructor.

cases.prompt: My teammate says we should split every class into tiny single-method classes because small classes are cleaner. Convince me whether this is right, using solid reasoning.
expectations: The agent rejects classitis with the depth argument: many tiny classes produce shallow modules whose interfaces cost more than the functionality they hide.
The agent explains complexity symptoms (change amplification, cognitive load, unknown unknowns) as the yardstick, not class count.
The agent acknowledges when splitting IS right (truly separable abstractions) instead of arguing the absolute opposite.
